cards.title: Performance Max campaign setup with category-specific asset groups
cards.summary: Build PMAX campaigns by splitting asset groups by product category, feeding Google matched headlines/imagery/landing pages, and using search and audience signals as a conversion flywheel.
cards.use_when: Launching or restructuring a Performance Max campaign for a store with multiple product categories (e.g. dresses, shoes, hats).
steps: Create an asset group per major product category rather than dumping all products into one asset group. Use listing group > 'selection of products' and filter by item ID to isolate that category's SKUs.
Fill brand guidelines (business name, logo, colors, fonts) so ad assets stay visually congruent.

Max out copy assets: 15 headlines, 5 long headlines, 5 descriptions — shortfall limits Google's combinations. (Agency uses an internal GPT to draft these; third-party tools may change, verify current availability.)
Supply up to 20 images: product, lifestyle, in-use, high-production; horizontal, square and vertical aspect ratios. Rotate weak images out over time.

Point the final URL to the matching collection page per asset group so searchers land on the exact category. If you use the brand homepage as final URL, Google can auto-route products — the source says test which approach works for your brand.

Load search themes (up to 50): your highest-volume, highest-converting terms pulled from Keyword Planner, existing search/shopping campaigns and demand-gen data. Add audience signals: customer lists, website visitors, competitive keywords/sites.
Set location to 'presence' only, select your language, and set brand exclusions as a first pass (source warns it is not foolproof; brand terms often need manual exclusion after launch).
Set budget at least $50/day, ideally $100/day, of what you can sustain.
caveats: Source says brand exclusions in settings are not a complete fix — expect to manually exclude branded search terms later.
Source disables tablets and TV screens for PMAX; TV screens only for dedicated demand-gen campaigns.
Source keeps only 'images' asset optimization on and disables text and final URL expansion to stop irrelevant landing-page text, sizing charts and support pages being pulled in.

cards.title: Daily PMAX search-term and auction-insight hygiene
cards.summary: Review PMAX search-term insights every day to exclude irrelevant queries, catch branded leakage, and harvest new profitable keywords for search campaigns.
cards.use_when: Daily check on a running Performance Max campaign to protect budget and reallocate targeting.
steps: Open the PMAX campaign > Insights and reports. Review search terms that triggered the ad over the last 7 and 28 days.
Flag and exclude irrelevant search terms directly inside PMAX to stop wasted spend. The source frames this as building a 'firewall' around the campaign.
Watch for branded conversions appearing in PMAX search terms — brand is supposed to be excluded; if branded terms show up, exclude them immediately through the additional brand-exclusion process.
Read cost per conversion and CTR by search term; treat rising costs or falling CTR as a signal that ad assets need refreshing.
Harvest terms converting in PMAX but not covered by your search campaigns as candidates for dedicated search campaigns.
Check auction insights (impression share on Search and Shopping, last 28 days) to see who you are competing against.
Use audience insights to feed what is working back into demand-gen campaigns and to see which audiences respond to which assets.
caveats: This is described as the source's only required daily PMAX task; everything else is weekly or monthly.

cards.title: Weekly PMAX product-level spend and SKU exclusion
cards.summary: Inspect which products actually receive PMAX budget weekly and exclude poor-performing or out-of-stock SKUs to protect efficiency.
cards.use_when: Weekly budget review for a Performance Max campaign with multiple products or categories.
steps: In the PMAX campaign, open the 'Products' view to see spend and performance at product level.
Confirm budget flows to best sellers and highest-margin products rather than defaulting to whatever Google picks.
Identify products that consume spend without converting, and products with weak CTR dragging the asset group down.
Exclude poor performers: Campaigns > Asset groups > View listing groups > exclude the specific products.
Keep excluded out-of-stock product pages out of PMAX until inventory returns — source lists removing out-of-stock URLs as part of exclusion hygiene.
Re-include a SKU only when you have inventory and want to test it again.
caveats: With a single-product brand the product-level view is trivial; the value appears when multiple products sit inside listing groups.

cards.title: Weekly asset and landing-page exclusions in PMAX
cards.summary: Refresh low-performing ad assets weekly and exclude non-converting URLs from final URL expansion to keep spend on sales pages.
cards.use_when: Weekly creative and traffic-routing review inside a live Performance Max campaign.
steps: Campaigns > Asset groups > View asset details to see conversion data, clicks, CTR and conversion rate per headline, long headline, description and image.
Replace assets that get little or no spend or weak conversion performance each week; Google prioritizes high-performing assets, so removing weak ones lifts overall results.

If automatically created assets or final URL expansion is on, exclude irrelevant URLs: blog posts, about pages, sizing/fitness charts, shipping info, contact and customer-service pages, and other support pages that kill purchase momentum.
Find which pages are currently being served: Report editor > 'when and where your ad shows' > PMAX campaigns placement; then add those unwanted URLs to exclusions.
Also check the landing-page report: Report editor > Ads and assets > Landing pages, and list pages with high spend but low conversion rate as first candidates for exclusion or replacement.
Use analytics to find high-bounce pages and add them to the exclusion list.
caveats: Source treats asset optimization text and final URL expansion as risky because they pull irrelevant page text; keep only image/layout asset optimization on.

cards.title: Monthly PMAX search-theme and customer-list refresh
cards.summary: Once a month, replace non-converting search themes with proven converters and re-upload your first-party customer list to sharpen signal quality.
cards.use_when: Monthly optimization cycle for PMAX audience and keyword signals.
steps: Pull top converting search terms from your search campaigns, shopping campaigns and PMAX itself.
Open Campaigns > Asset groups > edit signals and replace search themes that are not converting with the proven converting terms.
Confirm themes align with high-performing queries rather than legacy guesses.
Export new customer emails and phone numbers from your CRM (Shopify, Klaviyo etc.) for the previous period.
In Google Ads, go to Audience manager > your data segments > plus icon > Customer list > upload new list.
Set a monthly reminder to repeat, or automate the upload, so Google can find users similar to your best customers and improve retargeting effectiveness.
caveats: Customer-list targeting works from first-party data quality — stale or partial lists weaken the audience signal.

cards.title: Break-even CPA and ROAS as your scaling baseline
cards.summary: Calculate the maximum you can spend to acquire a customer (break-even CPA) and the corresponding break-even ROAS from your own unit economics before scaling any campaign.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether you can profitably increase Google Ads budget, bids or a new channel's spend.
steps: Compute break-even ROAS: 100 ÷ gross margin percentage. At 40% gross margin, break-even ROAS is 2.5; at 70% gross margin it is lower.
Compute break-even CPA: AOV × gross margin percentage − fixed COGS costs. Example given: $100 AOV at 40% gross margin means $40 is the maximum acquisition cost before losing money.
Set these as non-negotiable baselines for every campaign, including PMAX.

Recognize this is a CPM arbitrage: platforms charge what they charge for a customer on a given day; if your unit economics cannot sustain the cost per conversion, the fix is better margin, not a campaign setting.
Track new-customer CPA and ROAS (source calls new-customer ROAS the single most important KPI) alongside conversion rate and marketing efficiency ratio (total revenue ÷ total marketing spend).
caveats: Source explicitly refuses to give universal good/bad ROAS or CPA numbers — thresholds are entirely business-specific.
Break-even ROAS is described as less decision-useful than break-even CPA; compute both but scale on CPA against your margin.
Case-study figures elsewhere in the source (e.g. ~$45k spend at ~1.29x ROAS with $44.65 CPA) are that brand's results, not benchmarks.

cards.title: Weekly budget scaling rules with traffic-light KPIs
cards.summary: Use break-even CPA and ROAS to scale winners 10–20%, cut losers fast, and judge whether to raise budget or lower targets based on budget pacing.
cards.use_when: Weekly budget and bid decisions across Google Ads campaigns including PMAX.
steps: Assess KPIs weekly against your break-even CPA and break-even ROAS.
If ROAS is consistently above break-even and/or CPA trends below break-even CPA, increase budget 10–20% (source says you can go faster but does not recommend it) or raise bids to capture more volume.
Pause or rebuild anything below break-even — products, asset groups or individual assets.

If consistently spending 100% of daily budget while hitting KPIs, raise budget by 10–15%. If spending under 80% of daily budget and underperforming, lower tROAS or tCPA to widen reach and generate volume.
Cut fast, scale slow: pause losing campaigns quickly but also scale winners in controlled increments because Google reacts sensitively to abrupt changes.
Let bidding changes run 2–4 weeks before evaluating; avoid frequent tweaks.

Compare maximized conversions versus maximize conversion value with tROAS — conversion value prioritizes higher-value purchases and suits higher AOV products; source starts on maximize conversion value and moves to tROAS for PMAX, but says mileage varies.
Monitor marketing efficiency ratio across all channels (Meta, TikTok, organic, Klaviyo, Google) because a profitable PMAX can still fail to add incremental lift or cannibalize other channels.
caveats: 10–20% scale increments and 80%/100% budget-pacing thresholds are the source's heuristics, not derived calculations.
Source advises against large budget jumps despite acknowledging faster scaling can work.

cards.title: Device and placement rules for PMAX and demand gen
cards.summary: Turn off tablets always, keep mobile (highest-converting, highest-cost) and desktop on, and reserve TV placements for dedicated demand-gen campaigns.
cards.use_when: Setting device targeting for a Performance Max or demand-gen campaign.
steps: Turn off tablets for PMAX — the source never runs anything on tablets for any brand.
Turn off TV screens for PMAX; enable TV screens only for dedicated demand-gen/YouTube campaigns where the TV viewership matters.
Keep mobile phones on: source describes mobile as the highest-converting, highest-searching and highest-cost device.
Break the campaign down by device to see how computers compare with mobile. Keep desktop only if its metrics are strong; otherwise turn it off.
Consider that a large share of US YouTube views happen on TV screens, so excluding TV placements can forfeit a big chunk of reach — a reason to run TV on demand-gen rather than PMAX.
caveats: Device cost/conversion relationships vary by brand; the source instructs checking your own desktop performance rather than assuming.

cards.title: Where YouTube and demand gen sit in the Google Ads funnel
cards.summary: Structure campaigns as demand generation (top), prospecting search/shopping/PMAX (middle, capped by search volume), and branded/remarketing (bottom) so YouTube feeds the whole system.
cards.use_when: Auditing an account's campaign mix or deciding where to add YouTube/demand-gen spend.
steps: Top of funnel: demand gen campaigns run on YouTube Shorts and YouTube in-stream; Google Display is optional and higher risk. These generate demand and educate unaware/problem-aware audiences.

Middle of funnel: prospecting search, prospecting shopping and Performance Max — these capture demand and are capped by the available search volume and competitor CPC inflation. Do not mistake PMAX/search for top of funnel.
Bottom of funnel: branded search, branded shopping, homepage/product page, add-to-cart and dynamic remarketing via Merchant Center or a dedicated remarketing campaign.
Connect the layers: every drop-off point gets dynamic remarketing back to the relevant page; cart abandoners return to the product page.
Sequence expansion: launch branded and search campaigns first, then add YouTube demand gen to generate additional search volume that your existing search/shopping campaigns capture.
Treat YouTube as the accelerant that raises brand search volume and improves conversion rates on Meta and Google, not just a standalone channel.
caveats: The funnel split is the source's framework; actual incremental lift from YouTube is asserted via third-party incrementality studies, not measured in the course itself.

cards.title: Why YouTube ads scale past search-volume ceilings
cards.summary: Use YouTube demand gen for ecommerce when search/shopping demand is capped or CPCs are inflating, exploiting cheap CPM arbitrage and creative reuse.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether to open a new acquisition channel because search/shopping volume or margin is maxed out.
steps: Recognize the ceiling: Google search/shopping can only serve people actively searching, so spend is capped by search volume and rising competitor CPCs reduce profitability.
Target top-of-funnel viewers who have the problem but are not searching — educate them so they later search for your brand/product and hit your branded search and shopping campaigns.

Reuse creative that already works on Meta by adapting it for YouTube in-stream and Shorts; this taps customers who do not buy from Facebook/Instagram without adding more Meta spend that might be unprofitable.
Exploit CPM arbitrage: source claims YouTube CPMs/CPCs are far lower than Meta because fewer advertisers are sophisticated there — verify current rates in your own account rather than assuming.
Factor in durability: source reports YouTube creative lasting up to a year or two versus Meta creative fatigue, so fewer new assets are needed once a winner is found.
Value channel diversification both for stability (if one channel turns off) and for enterprise value at exit.
caveats: The CPM-arbitrage and 'creative lasts a year' claims are the source's observations for their client base, not guarantees.
YouTube is not a replacement for bottom-funnel brand control; it works with search/shopping to capture the generated demand.

cards.title: Choosing the right YouTube placement: Shorts, in-stream or in-feed
cards.summary: Start with YouTube Shorts and in-stream for volume and testing; treat in-feed as a later, higher-production placement.
cards.use_when: Allocating YouTube demand-gen budget across placements for an ecommerce brand.
steps: YouTube in-stream (skippable): the placement with the most scale and where the source spends thousands per day per client; best for proven winning creative.

YouTube Shorts: cheap CPMs and very cheap clicks (source cites 1–2 cent clicks), lots of volume, quick creative testing. Shorts winners usually also win on in-stream after tweaking, so test there first.
YouTube in-feed: higher production demand — requires a strong thumbnail competing against organic videos; only worth scaling once you have real creative quality or an organic channel.
Do not run Discover, Gmail or the Display Network for ecommerce YouTube — the source restricts YouTube to in-stream and Shorts (Display optional only at top of funnel if you accept the risk).

Note that in-feed suits longer, organic-style videos (the source cites buying competitors' products and reviewing them in an ~8-minute sponsored video with a CTA at the end); a 2-minute spot belongs in in-stream.
Budget the higher-production in-feed efforts after Shorts and in-stream are producing winners.
caveats: Click-cost and CPM figures are the source's observed ranges at the time of recording; verify current auction rates.
In-feed is explicitly described as lower-leverage and harder to get right for most ecommerce brands.

cards.title: YouTube in-stream creative structure and first 5 seconds
cards.summary: Because skipped in-stream ads guarantee only 5 seconds, front-load an audio+visual movie-trailer hook, then demo, social proof and a strong CTA to beat 1% CTR.
cards.use_when: Writing or editing YouTube in-stream ad creative for a cold ecommerce audience.
steps: Treat the first 5 seconds as fixed and non-skippable plus up to ~30 seconds before a view counts — the hook must be the strongest element you have and work both visually and in audio.
Use a movie-trailer style hook: assume the viewer is about to skip, so the ad must be compelling enough to make them abandon the video they intended to watch.
Structure after the hook: next ~5 seconds to introduce product or problem, then product demo showing use and effects, then social proof near the end, then a strong direct-response CTA.
Aim the whole ad at a direct-response outcome — you need high-intent clicks, not passive viewing; source targets above 1% CTR on in-stream.

Choose one of five creative types that work: high-production talking head, podcast-style two-person hook, founder ads (source calls founder ads a 'cheat code' and even suggests hiring someone to play the founder if dropshipping), story ads (customer- or founder-told) and straight product demos.
Avoid cheesy AI-generated UGC style with bad captions — source says it no longer works well on YouTube; authenticity and craft matter more here than on Meta.
caveats: Format timings (5s hook, ~30s to view) reflect the source's era of YouTube in-stream mechanics; verify current ad specs.
The '1% CTR' target is the source's own working target, not a platform benchmark.

cards.title: YouTube as brand-lift and TV-reach play
cards.summary: Use demand-gen YouTube placements partly for perceived legitimacy and TV reach, accepting view-through rather than direct-click conversions.
cards.use_when: Justifying and measuring upper-funnel YouTube spend for a brand that mostly converts later through search.
steps: Account for TV reach: source claims over 50–60% of US YouTube views happen on TV screens, so mobile-only or desktop-only buying misses roughly half the audience.
Operate with the expectation that TV viewers rarely convert immediately; they see the ad, search the brand later and convert through a view-through conversion.
Track view-through conversions as a meaningful signal, not noise, especially for podcast/creator-led creative.

Leverage perceived legitimacy: TV and YouTube placement is perceived as a higher barrier to entry, which the source says can lift conversion rates across Meta, Google search/shopping and retail (citing third-party incrementality studies).
Use brand lift studies where available rather than judging YouTube purely on last-click ROAS in-dashboard.
caveats: The TV-view share figure and incrementality effects are the source's cited claims, not measured in this course — validate with your own lift data.
View-through conversions can overstate causal impact; pair with account-level incrementality checks.

cards.title: Composite approach: standard shopping alongside PMAX
cards.summary: Test running standard shopping at a low tROAS with PMAX as a higher-tROAS catch-all, and mirror PMAX conversion data into dedicated search campaigns.
cards.use_when: Considering advanced Google Ads structures after a PMAX campaign has conversion data.
steps: Optionally run standard shopping at a low tROAS while PMAX works as a catch-all at a higher tROAS — source says this sometimes works and sometimes does not, so treat it as a test in your account.

Use PMAX conversion data to decide new search campaigns: if terms convert in PMAX but are not covered by existing search campaigns, build dedicated search campaigns around them for more control over the funnel and experience.
Note that PMAX consumes a lot of search spend; the Micros PPC script (Google Ads script) reveals this hidden spend and additional PMAX data for deeper optimization.
For product-aware versus problem-aware keyword choices, start search campaigns on product-aware terms and use PMAX data to extend into other converting terms.
For multi-location sellers, either run a dedicated Google Ads account per location or duplicate the PMAX campaign and change the location — horizontal scaling.
caveats: Source explicitly says the standard-shopping + PMAX combination is not a universal play and is used selectively.
Micros PPC is a third-party script; verify current availability and that it still works with the current Google Ads interface.
